title: History of Buddhism
wiki_lead:
The history of Buddhism can be traced back to the 5th century BCE. Buddhism originated in ancient India, in and around the Kingdom of Magadha, and is based on the teachings of the renunciate Siddhārtha Gautama. The religion evolved as it spread from the northeastern region of the Indian subcontinent throughout Central, East, and Southeast Asia. At one time or another, it influenced most of Asia.
The history of Buddhism is also characterized by the development of numerous movements, schisms, and philosophical schools. Among them were the Theravāda, Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna traditions, with contrasting periods of expansion and retreat.

The history of Buddhism can be traced back to the 5th century BCE. Buddhism originated in ancient India, in and around the Kingdom of Magadha, and is based on the teachings of the renunciate Siddhārtha Gautama. The religion evolved as it spread from the northeastern region of the Indian subcontinent throughout Central, East, and Southeast Asia. At one time or another, it influenced most of Asia.
The history of Buddhism is also characterized by the development of numerous movements, schisms, and philosophical schools. Among them were the Theravāda, Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna traditions, with contrasting periods of expansion and retreat.


Shakyamuni Buddha (5th cent. BCE)

Siddhārtha Gautama (5th cent. BCE) was the historical founder of Buddhism. The early sources state he was born in the small Shakya (Pali: Sakya) Republic, which was part of the Kosala realm of ancient India, now in modern-day Nepal. He is thus also known as the Shakyamuni (literally: "The sage of the Shakya clan").
The Early Buddhist Texts contain no continuous life of the Buddha, only later after 200 BCE were various "biographies" with much mythological embellishment written. All texts agree however that Gautama renounced the householder life and lived as a śramaṇa ascetic for some time studying under various teachers, before attaining nirvana (extinguishment) and bodhi (awakening) through meditation.
For the remaining 45 years of his life, he travelled the Gangetic Plains of eastern-central India (the region of the Ganges River and its tributaries), teaching his doctrine to a diverse range of people from different castes and initiating monks into his order. The Buddha sent his disciples to spread the teaching across India. He also initiated an order of nuns. He urged his disciples to teach in the local language or dialects. He spent a lot of his time near the cities of Sāvatthī, Rājagaha and Vesālī (Skt. Śrāvastī, Rājagrha, Vāiśalī). By the time of his death at 80, he had thousands of followers.


Early Buddhism

After the death of the Buddha, the Buddhist sangha (monastic community) remained centered on the Ganges valley, spreading gradually from its ancient heartland. The canonical sources record various councils, where the monastic sangha recited and organised the orally transmitted collections of the Buddha's teachings and settled certain disciplinary problems within the community. Modern scholarship has questioned the accuracy and historicity of these traditional accounts.
The first Buddhist council is traditionally said to have been held just after Buddha's Parinirvana, and presided over by Mahākāśyapa, one of his most senior disciples, at Rājagṛha (today's Rajgir) with the support of king Ajātasattu. According to Charles Prebish, almost all scholars have questioned the historicity of this first council.


Mauryan Empire (322–185 BCE)


Second Buddhist council and first schism

After an initial period of unity, divisions in the sangha or monastic community led to the first schism of the sangha into two groups: the Sthavira (Elders) and Mahasamghika (Great Sangha). Most scholars agree that the schism was caused by disagreements over points of vinaya (monastic discipline). Over time, these two monastic fraternities would further divide into various Early Buddhist Schools.
Lamotte and Hirakawa both maintain that the first schism in the Buddhist sangha occurred during the reign of Ashoka. According to scholar Collett Cox "most scholars would agree that even though the roots of the earliest recognized groups predate Aśoka, their actual separation did not occur until after his death." According to the Theravada tradition, the split took place at the Second Buddhist council, which took place at Vaishali, approximately one hundred years after Gautama Buddha's parinirvāṇa. grok_lead: The history of Buddhism traces the origins, doctrinal developments, geographic expansions, and institutional evolutions of a philosophical and religious tradition founded in the ancient Indian subcontinent by Siddhartha Gautama, who achieved enlightenment around the 5th century BCE in Bodh Gaya, India, and became known as the Buddha. He then taught for approximately 45 years across the Gangetic plain in northern India, delivering his first sermon at Sarnath (town northeast of Varanasi, in Uttar Pradesh, India), where he taught the Dharma to his initial disciples, establishing a monastic community (sangha) and expounding doctrines including the Four Noble Truths. Emerging amid the spiritual ferment of the Mahajanapadas (Great States), such as Kosala and Malla, of the ancient Indian subcontinent, Buddhism emphasized the Eightfold Path as means to end suffering through insight into impermanence, non-self, and dependent origination. The sangha preserved oral teachings later committed to texts. Following the Buddha's parinirvana (death in Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh, India) in the Malla Kingdom of ancient India, early councils sought to standardize doctrine, but schisms arose, leading to the formation of sects like the Sthavira and Mahasanghika lineages by the 4th century BCE. The tradition's pivotal expansion occurred under Mauryan Emperor Ashoka (r. c. 268â232 BCE), whose conversion after the Kalinga War prompted edicts promoting dhammaâethical principles aligned with Buddhist preceptsâand missions dispatching monks to Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and the Hellenistic world, including the Parthian Empire where Buddhist presence facilitated transmission eastward, and the Indo-Parthian Kingdom which supported Buddhist communities and syncretic art, evidenced by archaeological pillars and rock inscriptions that mark the first imperial endorsement of Buddhism as a civilizing force. Following Ashoka's initiatives, Buddhist traditions coexisted under the Shunga dynasty (185â73 BCE), while the Satavahana dynasty (c. 230 BCEâ220 CE) patronized Buddhism by building stupas and supporting monasteries. This patronage facilitated Theravada's entrenchment in Sri Lanka, where it preserved Pali Canon texts, while in northern India, particularly under the patronage of the Kushan Empire (c. 30 BCEâ375 CE), Mahayana innovations around the 1st century CE introduced bodhisattva ideals and expanded scriptures (sutras) appealing to laity, fostering adaptations via Silk Road trade routes to Central Asiaâflourishing in Sogdia and early Uyghur contexts with sites such as Ajina Tepe in Tajikistan, Fayaz Tepe near Termez in Uzbekistan, Kizil Caves in Xinjiang, Bamiyan and Nava Vihara in Afghanistanâand to East Asia, reaching China under the Han dynasty by the 2nd century CE and flourished during the Tang Dynasty (618â907 CE), Korea under the Goguryeo kingdom in the 4th century CE, and Japan during the Asuka period in the 6th century CE. Vajrayana, incorporating tantric practices for rapid enlightenment, developed later in India from the 7th century, influencing Tibetan lineages after its transmission there during the 8th-century imperial period under kings like Trisong Detsen of the Yarlung dynasty. Despite continued flourishing under dynasties such as the Gupta Empire (320â550 CE) and the patronage of the Pala Empire (750â1174 CE) in monastic universities like Nalanda until the 12th century, Buddhism's presence in the Indian subcontinent waned due to assimilation into resurgent Hindu traditions, withdrawal of royal support favoring Brahmanism, internal corruption in sanghas, and devastating raids by Turkic-Muslim invaders that razed viharas and libraries, such as the 1193 destruction of Nalanda, effectively ending organized Buddhism on the Indian subcontinent by the medieval era. Elsewhere, it thrived: Mahayana in East Asia evolved into Chan/Zen and Pure Land schools, Theravada dominated Southeast Asia through early centers such as Luy LÃ¢u in Vietnam's Red River Delta, which emerged by the late 2nd century CE, and Pyu city-states in present-day Myanmar, which embraced Buddhism to establish monarchies by the 5th century CE, as well as kingdoms such as Dvaravati (6thâ11th centuries) in Thailand and Pagan (9thâ13th centuries) in Myanmar, while Srivijaya (7thâ13th centuries) in Indonesia centered Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions and facilitated maritime Buddhist networks, and Vajrayana defined Tibetan and Mongolian practices, extending further west through Oirat migrations that established the Kalmyk Khanate (1630â1771) in the lower Volga region of European Russia, with contemporary Kalmykia remaining the westernmost Buddhist-majority region. Mongol rulers of the Ilkhanate in Iran patronized Buddhism by inviting scholars from India, Central Asia, and Tibet. Global dissemination accelerated in the 19thâ20th centuries through colonial encounters and Western scholarship, though historical narratives often rely on biased monastic chronicles requiring corroboration from epigraphy and archaeology for causal accuracy.
